Human brain.summary: The human brain is the central organ of the nervous system, and with the spinal cord, comprises the central nervous system. It consists of the cerebrum, the brainstem and the cerebellum. The brain controls most of the activities of the body, processing, integrating, and coordinating the information it receives from the sensory nervous system. The brain integrates sensory information and coordinates instructions sent to the rest of the body.

Consciousness.summary: Consciousness is being aware of something internal to one's self, or of states or objects in one's external environment. It has been the topic of extensive explanations, analyses, and debate among philosophers, scientists, and theologians for millennia. There is no consensus on what exactly needs to be studied, or whether consciousness can be considered a scientific concept. In some explanations it is synonymous with mind, while in others it is considered an aspect of it.

Earth.summary: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life. This is made possible by Earth being an ocean world, the only one in the Solar System sustaining liquid surface water. Almost all of Earth's water is contained in its ocean, which covers 70.8% of Earth's crust. The remaining 29.2% of Earth's crust is dry land, which is predominantly located within Earth's land hemisphere in the form of continental landmasses. Most of Earth's land is at least somewhat humid and covered by vegetation, while large ice sheets at Earth's polar deserts retain more water than Earth's groundwater, lakes, rivers, and atmospheric water combined.

Machine learning.summary: Machine learning (ML) is a field of study in artificial intelligence concerned with the development and study of statistical algorithms that can learn from data and generalize to unseen data, and thus perform tasks without being explicitly programmed.

CSS.summary: Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) is a style sheet language used for specifying the presentation and styling of a document written in a markup language, such as HTML or XML. CSS is a cornerstone technology of the World Wide Web, alongside HTML and JavaScript.

Sleep.summary: Sleep is a state of reduced mental and physical activity in which consciousness is altered and certain sensory activity is inhibited. During sleep, there is a marked decrease in muscle activity and interactions with the surrounding environment. While sleep differs from wakefulness in terms of the ability to react to stimuli, it still involves active brain patterns, making it more reactive than a coma or disorders of consciousness.

Rust.summary: Rust is a general-purpose programming language that emphasizes performance , type safety , concurrency , and memory safety . Rust supports multiple programming paradigms . It was influenced by ideas from functional programming , including immutability , higher-order functions , algebraic data types , and pattern matching . It also supports object-oriented programming via structs, enums , traits, and methods. Rust enforces memory safety (i.e., that all references point to valid memory) without a conventional garbage collector ; instead, memory safety errors and data races are prevented by the "borrow checker", which tracks the object lifetime of references at compile time .
Rust.source: Wikipedia article + built-in blueprint + DuckDuckGo tutorials (live internet)

subtopics.fn main(): Every executable starts in fn main(); functions are declared with fn, typed parameters and an optional -> return type.
subtopics.variables and mutability: let creates an immutable binding by default, and let mut makes it changeable, which keeps accidental changes out.
subtopics.ownership: Each value has exactly one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped automatically.
subtopics.borrowing and references: &value lends read-only access and &mut value lends write access; the compiler allows many readers or one writer at a time.
subtopics.structs: struct groups named fields into a new type, and impl blocks add methods to it.
subtopics.enums and match: An enum lists the possible variants of a value, and match must handle every variant, so no case is forgotten.
subtopics.traits: A trait describes shared behaviour that different types can implement, similar to an interface.
subtopics.error handling: Result<T, E> carries either a value or an error, and the ? operator passes errors up; Option<T> models a value that may be missing.
subtopics.Cargo: Cargo is the build tool and package manager: cargo new creates a project, cargo run builds and runs it.
subtopics.iterators: iter(), map, filter, sum and collect process collections in a chain without manual index loops.
subtopics.2006–2009: Early years: In 2006, Rust began as a personal project by Mozilla employee Graydon Hoare.
subtopics.2009–2012: Mozilla sponsorship: In 2009, Mozilla officially sponsored the project. Brendan Eich and other executives, intrigued by the possibility of using Rust for a safe web browser engine, placed engineers on the project including Patrick Walton, Niko Matsakis, Felix Klock, and Manish Goregaokar.
subtopics.2012–2015: Evolution: The following years were marked by substantial changes to the Rust type system . : 18:36 Memory management through the ownership system was gradually consolidated and expanded; by 2013, the garbage collector was rarely used, and was removed.
subtopics.2015–2020: Servo and early adoption: The development of the Servo browser engine continued in parallel with Rust, funded by Mozilla and Samsung . New features in Rust were tested out by the Servo team, and new features in Servo were used to give feedback back to the Rust team.
subtopics.2020–present: Mozilla layoffs and Rust F: In August 2020, Mozilla laid off 250 of its 1,000 employees as part of a corporate restructuring during the COVID-19 pandemic . The Servo team was disbanded.
subtopics.Syntax and features: Rust's syntax is similar to that of C and C++ , although many of its features were influenced by functional programming languages such as OCaml . Hoare has described Rust as targeted at frustrated C++ developers.
subtopics.Hello World program: Below is a "Hello, World!" program in Rust. The fn keyword denotes a function , and the println! macro (see § Macros ) prints the message to standard output .
subtopics.Variables: Variables in Rust are defined through the let keyword. The example below assigns a value to the variable with name foo of type i32 and outputs its value; the type annotation : i32 can be omitted.
subtopics.Block expressions and control flow: A block expression is delimited by curly brackets . When the last expression inside a block does not end with a semicolon, the block evaluates to the value of that trailing expression: Trailing expressions of function bodies are used as the return value:
subtopics.Pattern matching: The match and if let expressions provide pattern matching . For example, match can double an optional integer value if present, and return zero otherwise: Equivalently, this can be written with if let and else :
subtopics.Types: Rust is strongly typed and statically typed , meaning that the types of all variables must be known at compilation time. Assigning a value of a particular type to a differently typed variable causes a compilation error .
subtopics.Ownership and references: Rust's ownership system consists of rules that ensure memory safety without using a garbage collector. At compile time, each value must be attached to a variable called the owner of that value, and every value must have exactly one owner.
subtopics.User-defined types: User-defined types are created with the struct or enum keywords. The struct keyword denotes a record type that groups multiple related values. enum s can take on different variants at runtime, with their capabilities similar to algebraic data types found in functional programming languages.
subtopics.Pointers: The & and & mut reference types are guaranteed to not be null and point to valid memory.

HTML.summary: HTML, short for HyperText Markup Language, is the standard markup language for documents shown in a web browser. A page is a tree of elements written as tags, such as headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, tables and forms, wrapped inside html, head and body.

subtopics.<!DOCTYPE> and <html>: The doctype line tells the browser to use modern standards mode, and the html element is the root that holds the whole page; set lang on it for accessibility.
subtopics.<head>: The head holds information about the page rather than visible content: the title, character encoding, viewport settings, links to style sheets and scripts.
subtopics.<title>: The title element sets the text shown in the browser tab, in bookmarks and in search results, so every page needs exactly one.
subtopics.<meta>: Meta tags describe the page; meta charset UTF-8 makes text display correctly and meta viewport makes the layout fit phones.
subtopics.<body>: The body contains everything the visitor sees: headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists, tables and forms.
subtopics.headings and paragraphs: h1 to h6 mark headings from most to least important and p marks a paragraph; use one h1 per page to show the main topic.
subtopics.links and images: The a element makes a link with an href attribute, and the img element shows a picture with src and a text description in alt.
subtopics.lists: ul makes a bulleted list, ol a numbered list and li one item inside either of them.
subtopics.tables: A table is built from tr rows containing th header cells and td data cells; it is for data, not for page layout.
subtopics.<form>: A form collects input: label describes a field, input and textarea accept text, button submits, and the name attribute identifies each value.
subtopics.<script>: The script element runs JavaScript, either inline between the tags or from a file with src; placed at the end of the body it can use the elements above it.
subtopics.<style>: The style element holds CSS rules inside the page head so that the same markup can be coloured, spaced and laid out.
subtopics.semantic elements: header, nav, main, section, article and footer describe the role of each region, which helps search engines and screen readers.
subtopics.Web tutorial notes: Well organized and easy to understand Web building tutorials with lots of examples of how to use HTML , CSS, JavaScript, SQL, Python, PHP, Bootstrap, Java, XML and more. In this article, we've organized all the essential HTML concepts and paired them with clear, practical examples to help you see exactly how each element works in real-world scenarios. Note: If you want to learn HTML Concepts then check out HTML Tutorials . 1. Basic HTML Tags and Structure Html defines the structure of the webpage. A collection of HTML5 examples covering topics like paragraph, images, forms, tables etc. to help you understand how HTML elements are used to create web pages.

Music.summary: Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or otherwise expressive content. Music is generally agreed to be a cultural universal that is present in all human societies. Definitions of music vary widely in substance and approach. While scholars agree that music is defined by a small number of specific elements, there is no consensus as to what these necessary elements are. Music is often characterized as a highly versatile medium for expressing human creativity. Diverse activities are involved in the creation of music, and are often divided into categories of composition, improvisation, and performance.

Google Sheets.summary: Google Sheets is a spreadsheet program included as part of the free, web-based Google Docs Editors suite offered by Google. Google Sheets is available as a web application, as mobile apps for Android and iOS, and as a desktop application on ChromeOS. The service is compatible with Microsoft Excel file formats.

Aspect ratio (image).summary: The aspect ratio of an image is the ratio of its width to its height. It is expressed as two numbers separated by a colon, in the format width:height. Common aspect ratios are 1.85:1 and 2.39:1 in cinematography, 4:3 (originally) and 16:9 in television, and 3:2 in still photography. Other common display aspect ratios include 5:4 and 16:10. The 1:1 aspect ratio is used for square images, often seen on social media platforms like Instagram, and 21:9 is an "ultrawide" aspect ratio popular for gaming and desktop monitors.

Memory.summary: Memory is the faculty of the mind by which data or information is encoded, stored, and retrieved when needed. It is the retention of information over time for the purpose of influencing future action. If past events could not be remembered, it would be impossible for language, relationships, or personal identity to develop. Memory loss is usually described as forgetfulness or a disorder such as amnesia.

JavaScript.summary: JavaScript ( JS ) is a programming language and core technology of the Web , alongside HTML and CSS . Created by Brendan Eich in 1995, it is maintained by Ecma International 's TC39 technical committee, with related Web APIs maintained by W3C and WHATWG . In 2025, JavaScript was the most widely used programming language on GitHub . However, TypeScript , a statically typed superset of JavaScript that is stricter about types, overtook JavaScript on GitHub by August 2025. Web browsers have a dedicated JavaScript engine that executes the client code . These engines are also utilized in some servers and a variety of apps . The most popular runtime system for non-browser usage is Node.js .
JavaScript.source: Wikipedia article + built-in blueprint + DuckDuckGo tutorials (live internet)

subtopics.variables (let and const): const declares a value that is not reassigned and let declares one that can change; avoid the older var.
subtopics.functions: A function groups steps under a name with function name(parameters) { ... } and gives back a value with return.
subtopics.arrow functions: An arrow function is a short form, (a, b) => a + b, and is the usual choice for callbacks.
subtopics.arrays: An array is an ordered list written in square brackets; push adds an item and map, filter and reduce transform the whole list.
subtopics.objects: An object stores named values in curly braces, like { name: 'Asha', marks: 88 }, and you read them with dot notation.
subtopics.conditionals and loops: if and else choose between paths, while for, for...of and forEach repeat work over a range or a collection.
subtopics.the DOM: document.querySelector finds an element, and properties such as textContent and classList change what the visitor sees.
subtopics.events: addEventListener runs a function when something happens, such as click, input or submit.
subtopics.promises and async/await: A promise stands for a value that arrives later; async and await let you write waiting code, such as fetch requests, in a straight line.
subtopics.modules: import and export let you split a program into files and share only what is needed.
subtopics.Creation at Netscape: The first popular web browser with a graphical user interface , Mosaic , was released in 1993. The lead developers of Mosaic then founded the Netscape corporation, which released a more polished browser, Netscape Navigator , in 1994.
subtopics.Adoption by Microsoft: Microsoft debuted Internet Explorer in 1995, leading to a browser war with Netscape. On the JavaScript front, Microsoft created its own interpreter called JScript .
subtopics.The rise of JScript: Brendan Eich later said of this period: "It's still kind of a sidekick language. It's considered slow or annoying.
subtopics.Growth and standardization: During the period of Internet Explorer dominance in the early 2000s, client-side scripting was stagnant. This started to change in 2004, when the successor of Netscape, Mozilla , released the Firefox browser.
subtopics.Reaching maturity: Ambitious work on the language continued for several years, culminating in an extensive collection of additions and refinements being formalized with the publication of ECMAScript 6 in 2015.
subtopics.Trademark: "JavaScript" is a trademark of Oracle Corporation in the United States. The trademark was originally issued to Sun Microsystems on 6 May 1997, and was transferred to Oracle when they acquired Sun in 2009.
subtopics.Website client-side usage: JavaScript is the dominant client-side scripting language of the Web, with 98.9% of all websites using it for this purpose. Scripts are embedded in or included from HTML documents and can interact with the DOM and other web APIs.
subtopics.Libraries and frameworks: Over 80% of websites use a third-party JavaScript library or web framework as part of their client-side scripting. jQuery is by far the most-used. Other notable ones include Angular , Bootstrap , Lodash , Modernizr , React , Underscore , and Vue .
subtopics.Other usage: The use of JavaScript has expanded beyond its web browser roots. JavaScript engines are now embedded in a variety of other software systems, both for server-side website deployments and non-browser applications .
subtopics.JavaScript engine: The first JavaScript engines were interpreters of the source code , but modern engines use just-in-time compilation to improve performance. JavaScript engines are typically developed by web browser vendors, and every major browser includes one.
subtopics.Runtime system: A JavaScript engine must be embedded within a runtime system (such as a web browser or a standalone system) to enable scripts to interact with the broader environment.
subtopics.Features: The following features are common to all conforming ECMAScript implementations unless explicitly specified otherwise. The number of cited reserved words including keywords is 50–60 and varies depending on the implementation.
subtopics.Imperative and structured: JavaScript supports much of the structured programming syntax from C (e.g., if statements, while loops, switch statements, do while loops, etc.). One partial exception is scoping : originally JavaScript only had function scoping with var ; block scoping was added in ECMAScript 2015 with the keywords let and const .
subtopics.Weakly typed: JavaScript is weakly typed , which means certain types are implicitly cast depending on the operation used. Values are cast to numbers by casting to strings and then casting the strings to numbers.

Safety.summary: Safety is the state of being protected from harm or other danger. Safety can also refer to the control of recognized hazards in order to achieve an acceptable level of risk.

Active matrix.summary: Active matrix is a type of addressing scheme used in flat panel displays. It is a method of switching individual elements of a flat panel display, known as pixels. Each pixel is attached to a transistor and capacitor that actively maintain the pixel state while other pixels are being addressed, in contrast with the older passive matrix technology in which each pixel must maintain its state passively, without being driven by circuitry.

By design, C gives programmers relatively direct access to the features of typical CPU architectures, customized for the target instruction set .
C.source: Wikipedia article + built-in blueprint + DuckDuckGo tutorials (live internet)

subtopics.headers (#include): #include copies a header into your file; stdio.h provides printf and scanf, and stdlib.h provides malloc and free.
subtopics.main(): Every C program starts in int main(void); returning 0 tells the operating system that it finished successfully.
subtopics.variables and types: Variables must be declared with a type such as int, double or char before use, for example int total = 0;.
subtopics.pointers: A pointer stores the memory address of another variable; &x gives the address and *p reads or writes the value stored there.
subtopics.arrays and strings: An array is a fixed-size run of values like int scores[5]; a string is a char array that ends with a zero byte.
subtopics.functions: A function has a return type, a name and typed parameters, and it must be declared before it is called.
subtopics.structs: struct groups related fields into one type, such as a student with a name and marks.
subtopics.memory (malloc and free): malloc asks for memory at run time and free gives it back; forgetting free causes a memory leak.
subtopics.printf and scanf: printf prints formatted text using placeholders like %d for int and %.2f for double, and scanf reads input the same way.
subtopics.control flow: if, else, switch, for, while and do-while decide what runs and how often.
subtopics.Characteristics: C is an imperative, procedural language with a free-form source layout. Statements are terminated by semicolons and grouped into blocks using curly braces .
subtopics.\"Hello, world\" example: The "Hello, World!" program example that appeared in the first edition of K&R has become the model for an introductory program in most programming textbooks.
subtopics.Early developments: The origin of C is closely tied to the development of the Unix operating system, originally implemented in assembly language on a PDP-7 by Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson , incorporating several ideas from colleagues.
subtopics.K&R C: In 1978, Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie published the first edition of The C Programming Language . Known as K&R from the initials of its authors, the book served for many years as an informal specification of the language.
subtopics.ANSI C and ISO C: During the late 1970s and 1980s, versions of C were implemented for a wide variety of mainframe computers , minicomputers , and microcomputers , including the IBM PC , as its popularity increased significantly.
subtopics.C99: The C standard was further revised in the late 1990s, leading to the publication of ISO/IEC 9899:1999 in 1999, which is commonly referred to as " C99 ".
subtopics.C11: Work began in 2007 on another revision of the C standard, informally called "C1X" until its official publication of ISO/IEC 9899:2011 on December 8, 2011.
subtopics.C17: C17 is an informal name for ISO/IEC 9899:2018, a standard for the C programming language published in June 2018. It introduces no new language features, only technical corrections, and clarifications to defects in C11.
subtopics.C23: C23 is an informal name for the current major C language standard revision. It was known as "C2X" through most of its development.
subtopics.C29: C29 (C2Y) are informal names for the next major C language standard revision, after C23 (C2X), that is hoped to be released no later in the 2020s, hence the '2' in "C2Y".
subtopics.Embedded C: Historically, embedded C programming requires non-standard extensions to the C language to support exotic features such as fixed-point arithmetic , multiple distinct memory banks , and basic I/O operations.
subtopics.Definition: C has a formal grammar specified by the C standard. Line endings are generally not significant in C; however, line boundaries do have significance during the preprocessing phase.
subtopics.Character set: The basic C source character set includes the following characters: The newline character indicates the end of a text line; it need not correspond to an actual single character, although for convenience C treats it as such.

SQL.summary: Microsoft SQL Server is a proprietary relational database management system developed by Microsoft using Structured Query Language (SQL, often pronounced "sequel"). As a database server , it is a software product with the primary function of storing and retrieving data as requested by other software applications —which may run either on the same computer or on another computer across a network (including the Internet). Microsoft markets at least a dozen different editions of Microsoft SQL Server, aimed at different audiences and for workloads ranging from small single-machine applications to large Internet-facing applications with many concurrent users .

subtopics.CREATE TABLE: CREATE TABLE defines a table with named columns, types and constraints such as PRIMARY KEY and NOT NULL.
subtopics.INSERT: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...) adds new rows to a table.
subtopics.SELECT: SELECT chooses which columns to return, and FROM names the table; SELECT * returns every column.
subtopics.WHERE: WHERE keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition, using comparisons and AND, OR and NOT.
subtopics.ORDER BY and LIMIT: ORDER BY sorts the result, with DESC for largest first, and LIMIT keeps only the first few rows.
subtopics.UPDATE and DELETE: UPDATE changes values in existing rows and DELETE removes rows; always add a WHERE clause so only the intended rows are touched.
subtopics.JOIN: JOIN combines rows from two tables that share a matching column, such as students.course_id = courses.id.
subtopics.GROUP BY and aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise rows, and GROUP BY computes them once per group; HAVING filters the groups.
subtopics.constraints and keys: A PRIMARY KEY identifies each row uniquely and a FOREIGN KEY links a row to a row in another table.
subtopics.indexes: An index makes lookups on a column much faster at the cost of a little extra storage when writing.
subtopics.History: The history of Microsoft SQL Server begins with the first Microsoft SQL Server product—SQL Server 1.0, a 16-bit server for the OS/2 operating system in 1989—and extends to the current day.
subtopics.Currently: As of November 2025 , the following versions are supported by Microsoft: From SQL Server 2016 onward, the product is supported on x64 processors only and must have 1.4 GHz processor as a minimum, 2.0 GHz or faster is recommended.
subtopics.Editions: Microsoft makes SQL Server available in multiple editions, with different feature sets and targeting different users. These editions are:
subtopics.Architecture: The protocol layer implements the external interface to SQL Server. All operations that can be invoked on SQL Server are communicated to it via a Microsoft-defined format, called Tabular Data Stream (TDS).
subtopics.Data storage: Data storage is a database , which is a collection of tables with typed columns.
subtopics.Buffer management: SQL Server buffers pages in RAM to minimize disk I/O. Any 8 KB page can be buffered in-memory, and the set of all pages currently buffered is called the buffer cache.
subtopics.Concurrency and locking: SQL Server allows multiple clients to use the same database concurrently. As such, it needs to control concurrent access to shared data, to ensure data integrity—when multiple clients update the same data, or clients attempt to read data that is in the process of being changed by another client.
subtopics.Data retrieval and programmability: The main mode of retrieving data from a SQL Server database is querying for it. The query is expressed using a variant of SQL called T-SQL , a dialect Microsoft SQL Server shares with Sybase SQL Server due to its legacy.
subtopics.T-SQL: T-SQL (Transact-SQL) is Microsoft's proprietary procedural language extension for SQL Server.
subtopics.SQL Server Native Client (a.k.a. SNAC): SQL Server Native Client is the native client side data access library for Microsoft SQL Server, version 2005 onwards.
subtopics.SQL CLR: Microsoft SQL Server 2005 includes a component named SQL CLR ("Common Language Runtime") via which it integrates with .NET Framework .
subtopics.Service: SQL Server also includes an assortment of add-on services. While these are not essential for the operation of the database system, they provide value added services on top of the core database management system.
subtopics.SQL Server Agent: SQL Server Agent is a component of Microsoft SQL Server which schedules jobs and handles other automated tasks. It runs as a Windows service so it can start automatically when the system boots or it can be started manually.
subtopics.Machine Learning Services: The SQL Server Machine Learning services operates within the SQL server instance, allowing people to do machine learning and data analytics without having to send data across the network or be limited by the memory of their own computers.

code_examples:
-- recipe: schema
CREATE TABLE students (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    course TEXT NOT NULL,
    marks INTEGER CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100)
);

INSERT INTO students (name, course, marks) VALUES
    ('Asha', 'Finance', 88),
    ('Ravi', 'Accounting', 74),
    ('Meera', 'Finance', 93),
    ('Kabir', 'Economics', 67);

-- who scored 80 or more, best first
SELECT name, course, marks
FROM students
WHERE marks >= 80
ORDER BY marks DESC;

-- recipe: aggregate
CREATE TABLE sales (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    region TEXT NOT NULL,
    amount REAL NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO sales (region, amount) VALUES
    ('North', 120.50), ('North', 80.00), ('South', 200.25), ('South', 150.75), ('East', 99.99);

-- one summary row per region, keeping only regions that sold more than 150 in total
SELECT region,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(amount) AS total,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS average
FROM sales
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) > 150
ORDER BY total DESC;

Image.summary: An image or picture is a visual representation. An image can be two-dimensional, such as a drawing, painting, or photograph, or three-dimensional, such as a carving or sculpture. Images may be displayed through other media, including a projection on a surface, activation of electronic signals, or digital displays; they can also be reproduced through mechanical means, such as photography, printmaking, or photocopying. Images can also be animated through digital or physical processes.

Google.summary: Google LLC is an American multinational technology corporation focused on information technology, online advertising, search engine technology, email, cloud computing, software, quantum computing, e-commerce, consumer electronics, and artificial intelligence (AI). It has been referred to as "the most powerful company in the world" by the BBC, and is one of the world's most valuable brands. Google's parent company, Alphabet Inc., has been described as a Big Tech company.
